_comment: Policy and regulation records. EVERY record must carry sourceTier and a source URL. Only 'primary' records (regulator, municipality, or government publication) are seeded here. Media coverage flows through the live news feed instead, where it is badged as reported. See MAINTENANCE.md.

commitments.title: Alberta's four commitments
commitments.note: The province's own stated test for data centre development. A useful spine to assess any application against.
commitments.sourceName: Government of Alberta — AI Data Centres in Alberta

items.label: Albertans do not pay
items.detail: Project costs are not to be transferred to ratepayers or municipal taxpayers.

items.label: The grid comes first
items.detail: System reliability takes precedence over new large-load connections.

items.label: Water use is controlled
items.detail: Water consumption is constrained and subject to reporting.

items.label: Albertans share the upside
items.detail: Through municipal tax revenue, royalties, and the data centre computing equipment levy.

records.title: Alberta AI Data Centres Strategy — Powering the Future of Artificial Intelligence
records.summary: Provincial strategy to position Alberta as a preferred North American location for large-scale AI computing. Built on three pillars: power capacity, sustainable cooling, and economic growth. Sets a target of $100 billion in private investment over five years.
keyPoints: Three pillars: power capacity, sustainable cooling, economic growth
$100 billion private investment target over five years
Led by Alberta's Ministry of Technology and Innovation
records.relevance: Sets the policy intent every downstream regulation and municipal bylaw is responding to.

records.title: Alberta Data Centre Regulation
records.summary: Creates the framework for how data centres connect to and operate within Alberta's electricity system. Defines a 'large data centre' as one with demand of 75 MW or more, and establishes the tethered / bridged / untethered connection classes.
keyPoints: Large data centre = 75 MW or more of demand
Tethered projects (paired with dedicated new generation or storage) receive AESO assessment priority
Tethered projects cannot obtain system access above their associated generation capacity until that generation is in service
Bridged projects get temporary access for a maximum of three years, subject to conditions
AESO may impose system access criteria: site control, permitting, financing, and zoning approvals
Large and bridged data centres may be prioritised for curtailment during supply constraints
records.relevance: The single most important document for a DP review. Tethered vs bridged status determines an applicant's real grid position and timeline.

records.title: Bill 8 — Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2025
records.summary: Amends the Electric Utilities Act to clarify the regulatory framework for data centre development and to incentivise projects that supply their own power. Underpins the bring-your-own-generation approach.
keyPoints: Amends the Electric Utilities Act
Clarifies the framework for self-supplied and hybrid power models
Supports faster approval timelines for self-powered projects
records.sourceName: BLG — Canada–Alberta MoU and Bill 8 — law firm summary
records.relevance: The enabling legislation behind the self-supply incentive. Explains why applicants increasingly arrive with their own generation proposal attached.
records.tierNote: Legislation summarised by a law firm. Cite the Act itself before relying on this in a decision.

records.title: AI data centre levy — Financial Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 (No. 2)
records.summary: A levy on computer hardware for grid-connected data centres drawing 75 MW or more, structured to reward self-supply. Takes effect 31 December 2026 and is fully creditable against Alberta corporate income tax.
keyPoints: 2% levy on computer hardware for grid-connected data centres at 75 MW or more
Reduced to 1% for grid-connected facilities that generate their own power
0% for off-grid facilities
Fully creditable against Alberta corporate income tax
In effect from 31 December 2026
records.sourceName: BLG — Alberta AI data centre levy framework — law firm summary
records.relevance: The levy tier is a fast proxy for how an applicant has structured its power supply. Worth capturing on any DP file.
records.tierNote: Legislation summarised by a law firm. Cite the Act itself before relying on this in a decision.

records.title: AESO interim approach to large load connections
records.summary: An interim framework enabling up to 1,200 MW of large load connections through 2028 while maintaining system reliability. Demand has far exceeded the cap.
keyPoints: 1,200 MW interim cap for large load connections through 2028
Reported as fully allocated
Connection queue of 29 projects representing more than 16 GW of demand
Roughly 19,565 MW of data centre load requested against the cap
A bridging approach allows limited early connection under strict reliability conditions, including obligations to reduce consumption when the grid requires it
records.relevance: The binding physical constraint. An application without a credible grid position is not a near-term project regardless of its land use merits.

records.title: Canada–Alberta Memorandum of Understanding
records.summary: Commits both governments to expanding electricity capacity to support AI and data centre infrastructure, and aligns Alberta's initiatives with Canada's Sovereign AI Compute Strategy.
keyPoints: Joint commitment to expand electricity capacity
Aligns provincial initiatives with the federal Sovereign AI Compute Strategy
records.sourceName: BLG — Canada–Alberta MoU and Bill 8 — law firm summary
records.relevance: Signals federal-provincial alignment, which matters for projects seeking federal support alongside provincial approvals.
records.tierNote: Legislation summarised by a law firm. Cite the Act itself before relying on this in a decision.

records.title: Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy
records.summary: Federal strategy led by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada to expand domestic AI computing infrastructure. Announced in Budget 2024 with $2 billion over five years.
keyPoints: $2 billion over five years from 2024–25 (Budget 2024)
Three elements: mobilising private investment, public supercomputing infrastructure, and an AI Compute Access Fund
Budget 2025 proposed a further $925.6 million over five years from 2025–26 for sovereign public AI computing infrastructure
records.relevance: The federal funding and policy context an Alberta project may be positioning against.

records.title: Federal call for proposals — sovereign large-scale AI data centres
records.summary: A one-month federal intake seeking proposals for sovereign, large-scale AI data centres exceeding 100 MW. Selected proponents enter memoranda of understanding with the Government of Canada.
keyPoints: Intake ran 15 January to 15 February 2026
Threshold of more than 100 MW
MOU-based process exploring support mechanisms and intergovernmental coordination
Aimed at domestic firms and consortia
records.relevance: Applicants may cite participation in this process. Worth confirming rather than accepting at face value.

pathway.title: Build Your AI Data Centre — the province's approvals map
pathway.note: Alberta's own gateway listing the provincial approvals a data centre project may require. The DP review checklist is aligned to these headings.
